config.motion: This house would tax sugary drinks

points: Taxes change prices, prices change behaviour, especially on cheap habitual products.
Sugary drinks hit kids and lower-income families hardest; revenue can fund healthier options.
The tax is a nudge making price honest about downstream diabetes and heart disease costs.
Regressivity is a fair hit, but those families pay the steepest disease price.
His liberty point rests on a false picture of artificially low prices.
A tax is compulsion, not moral judgment; the house must justify it.
A sugary drink tax is regressive by design, falling hardest on those least able to absorb it.
Taxation is blunt: it punishes a can of soda while straining household budgets.
Silence is not consent to being taxed; the case is liberty, proportionality, burden of proof.
The mover concedes regressivity and offers promises, not proof; burden unmet.

verdict.keyDisagreement: Whether the Proposition met its burden of proof by justifying a regressive tax through health costs and revenue-funded alternatives, or whether that justification remained an unproven promise.
verdict.rationale: The Proposition wins because its rebuttal and clarity scores were stronger, with Amara directly answering the regressivity charge and reframing the liberty argument, while Victor's evidence score was notably lower. Although Victor kept the burden-of-proof frame clear, his case rested more on assertion than on meeting the Proposition's substantive responses.
